analysis.title: What the US midterm elections mean for healthcare and pharma
key_insights: ING sees a Democratic takeover of Congress as most likely for the 3 November midterms, with polls showing Democrats ahead by about 8 percentage points nationally. A Democratic clean sweep is not certain.

Both parties now treat pharma and biotech as a national security sector and want more domestic manufacturing and lower drug prices. They differ on method: Democrats lean toward Medicare price negotiation and non-tariff incentives for domestic manufacturing, Republicans toward most-favoured-nation (MFN) pricing and trade pressure.

Scenario 1, Republican revival: Trump faces fewer congressional obstacles to Medicaid restrictions and a limited federal role in insurance, and resists restoring enhanced ACA subsidies. The main risk is further coverage erosion, more uncompensated care at hospitals in Medicaid-heavy markets and weaker pharma volumes where patients lose coverage.

Under Scenario 1, pharma gets greater scope for MFN pricing and for tariff exemptions and company agreements tied to US manufacturing commitments. ING calls this the scenario with the greatest continuity in pharma policy, with clarity on direction but no relief from pricing or supply-chain pressure.

Scenario 2, Trump constrained: a Democratic House could obstruct, control committees and investigate. Bills restoring ACA subsidies or softening Medicaid cuts would face a Republican Senate and a Trump veto, so policy becomes more confrontational but not very different in practice.

Under Scenario 2, pharma would face scrutiny of MFN deals, tariffs and Medicare negotiation implementation. Narrower bipartisan measures on pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) and hospitals become possible, while broader reform likely stalls.

Scenario 3, Democratic clean sweep: Democrats would have the strongest platform to restore ACA subsidies, soften Medicaid cuts and make healthcare affordability a condition in budget and defence negotiations. ING expects lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs, wider coverage, and better hospital finances and prescription volumes.

Under Scenario 3, Democrats would likely slow MFN momentum by demanding transparency on the deals and challenging their design and cost. They would likely expand or speed up IRA Medicare drug-price negotiation and scrutinise launch prices and PBMs.

Under Scenario 3, stronger congressional protection of NIH funding, scientific institutions and FDA review capacity would support biotech and early-stage innovation. ING describes the outcome as mixed: more price pressure but a stronger public research base and a better-funded FDA.

For Europe, pressure on pharma to localise in the US persists in all three scenarios, since Democrats also see pharma supply chains as a national security issue and Trump keeps substantial executive authority over trade.

A Democratic clean sweep would demand more MFN transparency and add price pressure through Medicare negotiation. ING says this could lead European governments to slow-walk their own price negotiations, expecting MFN terms to be delayed or revised.

A Republican clean sweep would reinforce policy continuity and the pull of manufacturing investment to the US. Europe's competitiveness problem is most pronounced in that case. Without better commercialisation, deeper capital markets and harmonised regulation, Europe risks losing production to the US and intellectual property and partnerships to China.
The US imports more than half of its pharmaceuticals from China by volume (2023), and China's dominance in active pharmaceutical ingredients is unlikely to fade soon.

ING forecasts Chinese outlicensing above $250bn this year, nearly double 2025 deal value. Licensing restrictions are now more likely to come from Beijing, which is considering limits on acquisitions of biopharma platforms involving key technologies, than from Washington.

Chinese licensing deals continue in any scenario, especially if Republicans keep Congress. Under a Democratic clean sweep, Trump may focus more on foreign and trade policy and China could be targeted, meaning more scrutiny of licensing and slower, not negative, deal growth in 2027.

sector_views.rationale: A Republican win brings further coverage erosion and more uncompensated care in Medicaid-heavy markets. A Democratic sweep would lower premiums, widen coverage and improve hospital finances.

Both parties want lower drug prices and domestic manufacturing. A Republican win means policy continuity on MFN pricing. A Democratic sweep brings more price pressure through Medicare negotiation but slower MFN momentum.
A Democratic sweep would protect NIH funding and FDA review capacity, supporting early-stage innovation. Chinese outlicensing is forecast to keep growing under any scenario.

macro_indicators.interpretation: A Democratic takeover of Congress looks most likely, though a clean sweep is not certain.
Nearly double 2025 deal value despite geopolitical tensions. Dealmaking is expected to continue under any election outcome.

tension_points.bull_case: Under a Republican win, pharma gets clarity on policy direction and the most continuity, with MFN pricing and company agreements on manufacturing.
tension_points.bear_case: Under a Democratic clean sweep, pharma faces greater price pressure from expanded Medicare negotiation and more scrutiny of launch prices and PBMs, though research funding and FDA capacity improve.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A split Congress, where a Republican Senate and Trump veto would stall broader reform.

theme_stances.key_argument: Both parties share bipartisan goals on domestic manufacturing and lower drug prices, so policy risks differ only slightly by outcome.
theme_stances.evidence: the policy risks differ slightly depending on the outcome
